correctness.rationale: The disjoint prefix-sibling pairs give the lower bound because their strict predecessor layers agree. Exactly one completion of each prefix satisfies the orientation rule, and no alternating word does. The one- and two-step layers are disjoint; the only possible center overlap is the period-two case, which is unselected. At odd length the two selected second predecessors give the unique repeated length-(n-2) suffix; the unique sensor with that suffix in its interior positions gives the prefix. At even length suffix-pairs recognize the selected layers. For two pairs a reverse overlap would force the even-length middle word to alternate, with the entering step opposite its final step, contradicting selection; with one pair the missing one-step layer determines the next orientation. Once the prefix is known, the selected completion cannot be a predecessor of the other sibling: one step violates proper adjacency and two steps require a period-two word. Presence of that completion decodes the center. This uses at most five length-n labels and constant scans. For n=2 any source goes directly to the target if its last letter equals the target's first, otherwise in two shifts, and n=1 is complete in one step. Thus both boundary cases have coincident balls.
residual_risks: The finite run corroborates the construction and decoder, not a computer proof for arbitrary n. The complexity is measured in symbol operations on the reporting labels, as stated.

value.rationale: The result settles an exact optimum and supplies an efficient decoder in a natural shift network and observation model. The decoder proves a real obstruction can be resolved at the lower bound; unlike simply selecting one sibling per pair, it deals with coinciding predecessor signatures, distinguishes parity, and covers all feasible lengths.
residual_risks: The construction is specific to ternary proper words and does not claim a classification of all optimal codes or other radii.
